title: Pinocchio promises the Fairy to be good and to study, because he is tired of being a puppet and wants to become a good boy.
paragraphs: At first the good little woman began by saying that she was not the little Fairy with the blue hair: but then, seeing she had been found out and not wanting to keep up the pretence any longer, she finally admitted who she was, and said to Pinocchio:
“You little rascal of a puppet! How ever did you realise it was me?”
“It was how much I love you that told me.”
“You remember, don’t you? You left me as a little girl, and now you find me a woman; so grown-up that I could almost be your mother.”

“And I’m very glad, because then, instead of little sister, I’ll call you my mother. I’ve been longing for so long to have a mother like all the other boys!… But how did you manage to grow up so quickly?”
“It’s a secret.”
“Teach me: I’d like to grow a little too. Can’t you see? I’m still no taller than a soldo’s worth of cheese.”
“But you can’t grow,” replied the Fairy.
“Why?”
“Because puppets never grow. They are born puppets, live as puppets, and die as puppets.”
“Oh! I’m tired of always being a puppet!” cried Pinocchio, giving himself a slap on the head. “It’s time I became a man too…”
“And you will, if you earn it…”
“Really? And what can I do to earn it?”
“Something very easy: get into the habit of being a good little boy.”
“Aren’t I one already?”
“Far from it! Good boys obey, and you, instead…”
“And I never obey.”
“Good boys learn to love studying and working, and you…”
“And I, instead, hang about and wander around all year.”
“Good boys always tell the truth…”
“And I always tell lies.”
“Good boys go to school gladly…”
“And school gives me a stomach ache. But from today I mean to change my life.”
“Do you promise me?”
“I promise. I want to become a good little boy, and I want to make my father happy… Where can my poor father be now?”
“I don’t know.”
“Will I ever be lucky enough to see him again and hug him?”
“I think so: in fact, I’m sure of it.”

At this answer Pinocchio was so very happy that he took the Fairy’s hands and began kissing them so eagerly that he seemed almost beside himself. Then, raising his face and looking at her lovingly, he asked:
“Tell me, Mummy: so it isn’t true that you’re dead?”
“It seems not,” answered the Fairy, smiling.
“If you knew how much it hurt, and how tight my throat felt, when I read ‘here lies’…”

“I know: and that’s why I forgave you. Your true sorrow showed me that you had a good heart: and with children who have good hearts, even if they are a little naughty and have bad habits, there is always something to hope for: that is, you can always hope that they will return to the right path. That is why I came all this way to find you. I will be your mother…”
“Oh, how wonderful!” cried Pinocchio, jumping for joy.
“You will obey me and always do what I tell you.”
“Gladly, gladly, gladly!”
“Starting tomorrow,” added the Fairy, “you will begin by going to school.”
Pinocchio immediately looked a little less happy.
“Then you will choose a craft or a trade that you like…”
Pinocchio grew serious.
“What are you muttering under your breath?” asked the Fairy, sounding annoyed.
“I was saying…” the puppet mumbled quietly, “that it seems a little late for me to go to school now…”
“No, it isn’t. Remember that it is never too late to study and learn.”
“But I don’t want to learn a craft or a trade…”
“Why?”
“Because work seems like hard work to me.”

“My boy,” said the Fairy, “people who say that almost always end up either in prison or in hospital. You should know that everyone in this world, whether born rich or poor, has a duty to do something, to keep busy, to work. Beware of letting laziness take hold of you! Laziness is a terrible illness, and it must be cured at once, while we are still children; otherwise, when we are grown-up, it can no longer be cured.”
These words touched Pinocchio’s heart, and lifting his head eagerly, he said to the Fairy:
“I’ll study, I’ll work, I’ll do everything you tell me, because, after all, I’m tired of a puppet’s life, and I want to become a boy whatever it takes. You’ve promised me, haven’t you?”
“I’ve promised you, and now it’s up to you.”
